title: Natural Law and Situation Ethics
welcome_lead: Set Aquinas's medieval synthesis against Joseph Fletcher's mid-twentieth century manifesto for love-based ethics.
meta_desc: A-Level Religious Studies adventure on Natural Law and Situation Ethics: primary precepts, double effect, Fletcher's six propositions.
final_note: You have contrasted rule-based and love-based Christian ethics on their foundational claims.

concepts.def: The rational participation in eternal law that human beings can discern by reason.
Self-preservation, reproduction, education, society, worship of God.
Aquinas's distinction between what truly perfects human nature and what merely seems.
An act with foreseen bad effects may be permissible if the act itself is good, the bad effect is unintended, the good does not flow from the bad, and there is proportionate reason.
Self-giving love; the only intrinsic good for Fletcher.
For Aquinas, the application of moral knowledge to particular acts; for Fletcher, the loving response in situation.

walkthroughs.body_html: In Summa Theologiae I-II QQ.90-97, Aquinas presents the four tiers of law and the primary precepts. Practical reason naturally pursues real goods rooted in human nature. Secondary precepts (no murder, no theft, etc.) are deduced from these. Acts are judged by object, intention and circumstance; intrinsically evil acts can never be justified.

The classic case: removing a cancerous womb that kills a foetus is permissible (the act is the removal of disease; the foetal death is unintended). Direct abortion is not (the act intends the death). Critics argue the distinction can be artificial; Philippa Foot's The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of Double Effect (1967) probed this with the trolley case.

Joseph Fletcher's Situation Ethics (1966) proposes six fundamental claims: only love is intrinsically good; the ruling norm is love; love and justice are the same; love wills the neighbour's good; only the end justifies the means; love decides situationally. Four working principles - pragmatism, relativism, positivism, personalism - frame his approach.
